title: Film: Fictional genres
notes: Cited for: genres promise something similar to past enjoyment yet new; viewers knew what to expect; a new film's success boosted by earlier genre films; studios reused sets and kept the same personnel on a genre; genres defined by subject or setting; the musical can be about almost any subject; acclaimed films invoke conventions to break them; Unforgiven's ironic perversion of the western's codes.

title: Western (genre)
notes: Cited for: the western's setting and period; basically an American creation; The Great Train Robbery set the pattern; cowboys, sheriffs and marshals; conflicts settled by violence; TV westerns of the late 1950s and 1960s; pioneers and Native Americans as a basic theme; earlier depictions lacking understanding; the later shift in sympathy.

title: Stagecoach (National Film Registry essay by Scott Allen Nollen)
notes: Cited for: the western had long been relegated to B status; Ford had not made a western in over a decade; Stagecoach's success revitalized a genre invented in the United States.

title: Musical film
notes: Cited for: definition of the musical film; Busby Berkeley's elaborate numbers within well-worn stories; singing and dancing teams such as Astaire and Rogers in Top Hat (1935); the late-1930s trend toward unifying plot and music, including The Wizard of Oz (1939).

title: Busby Berkeley
notes: Cited for: Berkeley placed the camera directly above his performers to show precise geometric formations; 42nd Street (1933) and his early-1930s peak at Warner Brothers.

title: Fred Astaire
notes: Cited for: Astaire simplified the movie musical, shooting dancers in full figure with a minimum of edits and camera angles; his RKO routines with Ginger Rogers as sophisticated statements of romantic love.

title: Singin' in the Rain (film, 1952)
notes: Cited for: 1952 MGM musical directed by Gene Kelly and Stanley Donen; Kelly's title number, swinging from a lamppost while celebrating new love.

title: Singin' in the Rain (film) (Research Starters, Mia Minichiello)
notes: Cited for: in Singin' in the Rain, song and dance rather than dialogue communicate the important moments.

title: It Happened One Night (film by Capra, 1934)
notes: Cited for: 1934 Capra comedy about a runaway heiress and a reporter; first film to win all five major Academy Awards.

title: Howard Hawks: Films of the mid-1930s
notes: Cited for: screwball conventions (mismatched lovers, off-the-wall characters, zany situations) established by Twentieth Century and It Happened One Night; overlapping dialogue as a Hawks trademark; His Girl Friday's rapid-fire dialogue and its change of The Front Page's editor and reporter to a man and a woman.

title: Romantic comedy (film)
notes: Cited for: screwball couples in Art Deco settings whose shared mischief proves them suited as lovers; Depression-era studios facing declining attendance; the Hays Code (1934 to 1968) and verbal sparring taking the place of sexuality.

title: Bringing Up Baby (film, 1938)
notes: Cited for: 1938 Howard Hawks screwball comedy in which Katharine Hepburn's eccentric heiress pursues Cary Grant's bookish paleontologist through farcical mishaps.

title: Horror film
notes: Cited for: definition of a horror film as calculated to cause intense repugnance, fear or dread.

title: Haunted House Researchers Investigate Playing with Fear
notes: Cited for: the 2020 Psychological Science field study of 110 visitors to a haunted house in Vejle, Denmark; recreational fear defined; inverted-U relation between fear and enjoyment; comparison with play.

title: Cat People (film, 1942)
notes: Cited for: 1942 low-budget horror film produced by Val Lewton for RKO; Irena is never shown in cat form; reliance on suggestion and imagination; shadows and low lighting to create suspense.

title: Cat People (National Film Registry essay by Chuck Bowen)
notes: Cited for: Lewton's suggestive horror made on skeletal budgets for RKO; silence held for long periods to build dread.

title: Film noir
notes: Cited for: French critics coined the term after World War II; American films banned in occupied countries reached Europe from 1946; stark high-contrast lighting and the isolated hero; German Expressionist roots; rain-soaked streets and neon; postwar disillusionment; European directors as outsiders; noir as a style rather than a distinct genre, applied to some westerns and comedies.

title: The Maltese Falcon (film, 1941)
notes: Cited for: John Huston's directing debut, adapted from Dashiell Hammett's 1930 hard-boiled detective novel; considered by some the first major work of noir.

title: Double Indemnity (film by Wilder)
notes: Cited for: 1944 Billy Wilder film adapted from James M. Cain's novel, co-written with Raymond Chandler; the audience knows who committed the crime from the start, making it a character-driven drama rather than a mystery.

title: The Day the Earth Stood Still (film, 1951)
notes: Cited for: 1951 Robert Wise film; Klaatu lands in Washington, D.C., and warns that humanity's atomic weapons threaten other civilizations; reflects Cold War and atomic-age anxiety.

title: Them! (film by Douglas, 1954)
notes: Cited for: 1954 Gordon Douglas film in which giant ants mutated by atomic bomb tests in the New Mexico desert threaten humanity; arguably the best of the 1950s giant atomic-mutant creature movies.

title: Invasion of the Body Snatchers (film by Siegel, 1956)
notes: Cited for: 1956 Don Siegel film; seedpod aliens take over sleeping people's bodies, leaving duplicates without emotion; read as an allegory of Cold War paranoia, McCarthyism, mass-society alienation or communism; Siegel denied political intent.

title: Truffaut par Truffaut: Truffaut / Hitchcock
notes: Cited for: Truffaut proposed the book to Hitchcock in 1962 and interviewed him at length; Le Cinéma selon Alfred Hitchcock was published by Robert Laffont in 1966.

title: Hitchcock, Lessing, and the bomb under the table (Observations on film art)
notes: Cited for: Hitchcock's bomb-under-the-table example from the Truffaut interviews (15 seconds of surprise versus 15 minutes of suspense; the audience participating in the scene).

title: Blazing Saddles (film by Brooks, 1974)
notes: Cited for: 1974 Mel Brooks spoof of westerns with a Black sheriff (Cleavon Little), satirizing racial prejudice and western conventions.

title: Young Frankenstein (film by Brooks, 1974)
notes: Cited for: 1974 Mel Brooks parody of Universal's Frankenstein films; black-and-white cinematography replicating the look of Bride of Frankenstein (1935).

title: Clint Eastwood: Films of the 1990s
notes: Cited for: Unforgiven (1992) as a revisionist western with an unsentimental look at frontier violence; Academy Awards for best picture and best director.
